passage: Four leads faced a junior teammate whose work kept slipping. Varun wrote down what had actually happened over a month: tasks handed in late three times and changes released twice with no testing. He kept words like careless out of it, so the talk would stay on the work itself. Damini took another route. In a private chat she asked, "What is making the tasks hard?" The junior admitted he could not follow the codebase and was afraid to ask, so the trouble was support, not effort. Pooja saved her deadlines a different way: at night she rewrote Arjun's code and kept it to herself. He never found out what had been wrong, and by the end of the month Pooja was exhausted while his work stayed the same. Neel had watched a junior for six weeks. The backend work was patchy, but the testing was excellent. With the manager's nod, Neel moved him into a quality role, and the junior's work steadied.

qa.q: What did Varun write down before talking to the junior?
qa.a: He wrote down tasks handed in late three times and changes released twice with no testing.

qa.q: How did Pooja's handling of Arjun's code differ from Damini's private talk, and what happened?
qa.a: Damini asked what made the tasks hard and learned the junior needed support and feared asking. Pooja rewrote Arjun's code in secret, so he learned nothing and she burned out.

qa.q: What might the junior have been afraid of when he did not ask for help?
qa.a: He was probably afraid of looking incapable or being judged, which kept him quiet about not understanding the codebase.

qa.q: What could Pooja do differently starting tomorrow?
qa.a: She could talk to Arjun openly, show him what went wrong in his code, and agree on a step to help him improve. Sharing the load with the manager would also protect her energy. 🙂

grounding: Four team leads handle an underperforming junior by collecting facts, finding the cause together, quietly redoing the work, and changing the role to fit strengths.
